claim: A circuit is an instruction vector with quantum and classical register widths; instructions include gates, measurement, reset, barriers, conditionals, regions and saves.
derivation: Gate and conditional targets use SmallVec<[usize; 4]>, preserving inline storage for four indices.
limitations: Classical dependencies and nonunitary instructions cannot be modeled by unitary composition alone.

claim: Fused and batched matrices use boxed payloads to retain a 16-byte gate enum.
derivation: Fused stores a 2 by 2 matrix, Fused2q stores a 4 by 4 matrix, and MultiFused and Multi2q store batches.
limitations: A tiled batch need not be one dense unitary over all its targets.

claim: Host fusion performs guarded bodies, cancellation, Rzz recognition and batching, 1q fusion, 1q reorder, cancellation, 1q fusion, 2q absorption and same-pair fusion before choosing staging or batching.
derivation: Listed in the order the host branch runs them. Each pass keeps its own width threshold.
limitations: The supports_fused=false entry bypasses all fusion. Tests use lower thresholds than native runs.

claim: Native buffer-width floors are 10 for general fusion, 12 for 2q fusion, 14 for multi-1q and diagonal batches, 16 for Pauli batches, and 18 for post-phase rebatching on wider buffers.
derivation: Post-phase rebatching on a buffer equal to circuit width instead uses the diagonal floor of 14.
limitations: The floors compare against buffer width, which is twice the logical width for density matrices. Stage planning can take the place of batching.

claim: Host fusion switches to tile staging once its own-width statevector exceeds a cache-derived floor.
derivation: The floor is floor(log2(LLC bytes / 16)) + 1, at least 16, with fallback 20; stages_at also requires equal circuit and buffer widths and at most 64 qubits.
limitations: The floor depends on detected host cache. The scheduler is heuristic and stops segments at nonbatchable instructions.

claim: Device fusion keeps an isolated CX and its neighbouring 1q gates as they are instead of folding them into a dense 4 by 4 gate.
derivation: Two-qubit absorption is restricted to members of same-pair runs; device lowering schedules its own tiles.
limitations: This covers the compiler profile only, not CUDA kernel scheduling or speed.

claim: Chronological gates G1, G2, G3 fuse to G3 times G2 times G1.
derivation: Column-state evolution applies each new matrix on the left.
limitations: Order cannot be reversed for noncommuting gates.

claim: Diagonal 1q gates can reorder past CX on the control and CZ or Rzz on either target, with explicit dependencies preserved.
derivation: Separate blockers track all 1q gates and diagonal gates for each qubit.
limitations: Only these listed rules apply; there is no general symbolic commutation. A CX target blocks diagonal movement.

claim: CX, CZ and SWAP pairs cancel when no intervening instruction touches their qubits; reversing CX targets does not preserve the operation.
derivation: CZ and SWAP admit target reversal while CX requires matching ordered targets.
limitations: The pass handles self-inverse two-qubit gates only. Other cancellations can fall out of later matrix fusion.

claim: A full read/write sweep of a complex128 statevector transfers 32 times 2^n bytes of amplitude payload.
derivation: 2^n amplitudes times 16 bytes per complex128 amplitude times one read and one write.
limitations: Payload only, not measured DRAM traffic. Cache reuse, specialized gates and batching all change the real figure. Dividing by an assumed bandwidth gives a lower bound on time.

claim: The base automatic family tree checks no entanglement, Clifford structure, statevector cap, sparse viability, partial independence, then dense statevector.
derivation: The branches select ProductState, Stabilizer, Sparse or Mps, Factored and Statevector respectively.
limitations: Terminal-specific routes, noise, decomposition and initial-state requirements can supersede this base tree.

claim: Above the statevector cap, automatic sparse selection accepts structural sparsity or a probe that stays at no more than 128 entries, within usize index width.
derivation: The probe applies gates to a sparse backend initialized at zero and tests entry_count after each operation.
limitations: The probe rejects resets, saves, and measurement arrangements that are not terminal.

claim: The public plan(Query) API reports the planned backend, rule, placement, exactness, alternatives, fallbacks, memory estimate and predictable failures.
derivation: Each terminal is represented by Query, allowing distinct plans for probabilities, shots, expectations and diagnostics.
limitations: Plans list possible runtime fallbacks separately. Memory excludes circuit storage, allocator overhead and process memory; Unknown has no byte count.

claim: Shot and expectation routes can use compiled Clifford sampling, stabilizer-rank paths, deterministic Pauli propagation and tensor contraction instead of the base backend family.
derivation: Terminal route decisions inspect requested results and circuit structure before generic backend execution.
limitations: A non-Clifford gate does not force dense simulation. Each route still has its own eligibility checks and budgets.

claim: Sparse simulation stores basis indices and amplitudes in FxHashMap with a retained swap map and a default squared-magnitude pruning threshold of 1e-28.
derivation: Memory scales with support plus map overhead; affected gates prune small entries and rescale retained amplitudes.
limitations: Width is limited by usize::BITS, dense Gate::Unitary is unsupported, and Hadamards can grow support exponentially.

claim: Factored simulation holds a dense substate per entangled group and merges groups when a gate bridges them.
derivation: Group storage sums 2^group_width complex amplitudes; global qubits map into sorted local group coordinates.
limitations: A highly entangled circuit can merge every qubit into one dense group. Measurement and reset splitting is subject to a seven-qubit floor.

claim: MPS stores site tensors shaped (chi_left, 2, chi_right); local gates act on sites and nonadjacent pairs use SWAP routing.
derivation: The flat tensor index is alpha*(2*chi_right) + physical*chi_right + beta.
limitations: Cost depends on bond dimension and routing as well as qubit count. Dense output still needs 2^n storage.

claim: SVD truncation keeps singular values strictly above epsilon times the largest, retains at least one, and applies the bond cap.
derivation: The implementation computes a relative threshold then limits retained rank; native default epsilon is 1e-12.
limitations: It bounds singular values, not discarded probability or global accuracy.

claim: MPS accumulates discarded squared singular weight divided by total squared weight for each SVD cut.
derivation: The cumulative value adds sum(discarded s_i^2)/sum(all s_i^2) over cuts; result queries normalize the state.
limitations: The sum can exceed one and does not measure final state error. The per-cut weights rely on the implementation's orthogonality-center handling.

claim: The reported MPS fidelity floor is a first-order estimate, not a certificate of final infidelity.
derivation: The field reports max(0, 1-sum(local discarded weights)); conservative accumulated error involves the square of summed square roots.
limitations: Error from many successive cuts accumulates differently from a single cut, so the field name overstates what it guarantees.

claim: The tensor-network backend appends gate tensors, plans contractions from metadata and can use exact index slicing or optional bounded contraction.
derivation: Seeded restarts can reduce peak intermediate size; slicing sums fixed-index assignments exactly. Positive tolerance permits rank reduction before replanning.
limitations: Slicing trades extra work for lower peak memory, and bounded contraction gives up exactness. Arbitrary circuits can still be expensive.

claim: Existing tests compare fused and unfused complex states and separately check staged execution, dependency rules and matrix composition order.
derivation: The unfused reference calls backend.apply directly, while the fused comparison uses sim::run_on; integration tolerance is 1e-10.
limitations: Reading the tests shows what they cover. It does not show that they pass on a later revision.

claim: Bench circuits use seed 0xDEAD_BEEF; shared Criterion configuration defaults to 30 samples with a ten-sample fast tier.
derivation: PRISM_BENCH_SAMPLES can override the sample count with a minimum of ten; fast groups use short warmup and measurement windows.
limitations: This is harness configuration; the atlas contains no benchmark results. Fast-tier numbers are for triage only.

claim: The A/B and same-binary interleaved scripts distinguish PASS, FAIL, host-busy and RERUN states, with a default 5 percent regression threshold.
derivation: Separate-binary comparison and interleaved coarse-switch comparison use controls to detect unresolved host or layout variation.
limitations: Only PASS and FAIL are results. RERUN and host-busy runs say nothing about performance.
